about.title: Shafter Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Shafter's economy leans heavily on agriculture, food processing, and logistics, all of which carry real physical risk. Whether you work a packing line, drive delivery routes past Zerker Road and 7th Standard Road, or handle machinery at a processing facility, an on-the-job injury usually means filing a workers' compensation claim through your employer first. But workers' comp isn't the whole story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to what happened to you, California law allows a separate claim against that third party. This matters in a place like Shafter, where many jobs involve outside contractors, delivery trucks, and shared job sites. We review the details of your situation, sort out what workers' comp covers, and identify whether a third-party claim applies. Our free case review comes with no obligation to move forward.

items.title: Third-Party Claims Aren't Blocked by Workers' Comp
items.desc: California generally makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or another driver — can still be held separately accountable.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter Early On
items.desc: California requires you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate your claim before it even starts.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal, and Deadlines Still Apply
items.desc: Employers can't legally punish you for reporting an injury, and if a third-party claim is involved, California generally gives you two years to pursue it.

items.question: I got hurt on a job site involving a contractor from outside my employer. Does workers' comp still apply?
items.answer: Workers' comp typically still covers you through your own employer regardless of fault. However, if a subcontractor or another company's negligence contributed to the incident, that opens the door to a separate third-party claim. We can look at how the job site was structured to figure out who else might be responsible.

items.question: Does Shafter's mix of agricultural and logistics work change how these claims are handled?
items.answer: The type of work doesn't change the underlying law, but it does affect who else might be involved — equipment suppliers, transport companies, or property owners along routes like Santa Fe Way or 7th Standard Road. That's part of why case-specific review matters.

items.question: What if I'm afraid my employer will retaliate if I report my injury?
items.answer: California law prohibits retaliation against employees for reporting a workplace injury, so taking action to protect your health and your claim is your right. If you're worried about how your employer might respond, we can advise you on next steps.
